name: Topical estrogen (estriol) cream

card.summary: A weak estrogen cream discussed for skin thickness; menopausal skin data exist, appearance-use data are thin.
card.note: Hormone product; generally prescription-only, with estrogen-class effects.

quick.overview:
Estriol is a mild natural estrogen used mainly in menopausal therapy. Creams are promoted for skin thickness and collagen.

Wikipedia reports research showing it can reverse postmenopausal skin thinning; facial appearance trials in other groups were not found.
quick.mechanism: Estriol activates estrogen receptors but more weakly than estradiol, acting as a partial agonist.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated; reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia. It is generally prescription-only.

lead: Estriol (E3) is a weak natural estrogen, one of the three major human estrogens alongside estradiol and estrone, used mainly in menopausal hormone therapy. It is sold as tablets, vaginal creams and suppositories and as skin creams, some over the counter and some from compounding pharmacies.[1][2]

In appearance circles, topical estriol is discussed as a way to counter the thinning and loss of collagen that skin undergoes after menopause, with the aim of firmer, thicker, smoother-looking skin. Wikipedia reports that research has found estriol can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen content.[2]

A 1996 controlled clinical trial in the International Journal of Dermatology examined topical estrogen treatment (0.01% estradiol and estriol preparations) for skin aging in perimenopausal women, prompted by the coincidence of menopausal symptoms and the onset of skin aging.[3] Estriol as a medicine is generally prescription-only, and as an estrogen it carries estrogen-class effects.

chain: Thicker skin with more collagen, firmer and smoother looking (reported in postmenopausal skin)
angle.text: Topical estriol is used by some people to restore skin thickness and collagen after the estrogen decline of menopause, aiming for firmer, smoother skin. Evidence reported for this comes from postmenopausal skin.

infobox: Generally prescription-only; some skin creams OTC or compounded[2]

paras: Estriol skin creams are marketed over the counter and by compounding pharmacies for aging skin.[2] The stated goal is to restore skin thickness, collagen content and firmness lost after menopause.[2][3]

Estriol is used for menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes, vaginal atrophy and painful intercourse, and has been linked to fewer urinary tract infections; vaginal use is well established, with much higher vaginal than oral bioavailability. Its effects on bone density are described as inconsistent.[2] Reviews of estriol's clinical benefits and of ultra-low-dose estriol vaginal gels in postmenopausal women have been published.[4][5]

Estriol is generally well tolerated. Reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation, burning, itching or discharge with vaginal use. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia, though typical vaginal doses appear to carry little of this risk.[2]

Estriol activates both estrogen receptors, ER-alpha and ER-beta, but is much less potent than estradiol and acts as a partial agonist, so it can weakly mimic estradiol or partly block it when both are present. It binds poorly to sex hormone-binding globulin and is cleared by glucuronidation and sulfation, mainly through urine.[1]

Estriol was discovered in 1930, isolated and purified from the urine of pregnant women by Marrian and colleagues, and was introduced for medical use soon after.[1][2] It is generally prescription-only, with Ovestin as the main brand.[2]

A 1996 controlled clinical trial in perimenopausal women examined whether topical estrogen (0.01% estradiol and estriol preparations) could reverse some changes of aging skin.[3] Wikipedia states that research shows estriol reverses the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen.[2] No studies were found testing estriol cream for facial appearance in non-menopausal users.

timeline.event: Estriol isolated from pregnancy urine by Marrian and colleagues.[1]
Controlled clinical trial of topical estrogens for skin aging in perimenopausal women published.[3]
Review 'Estriol: emerging clinical benefits' published in Menopause.[4]
